The New York Stock Exchange (NYSE) has picked Avalanche as the only blockchain to settle tokenized stocks on its planned 24/7 trading platform, The Wall Street Journal reported on Monday.

Tokenized stocks are blockchain tokens that track shares of real companies. The NYSE version would let investors trade U.S. stocks around the clock, settle trades instantly and pay with stablecoins, digital tokens that hold a steady $1 value.

The New York Stock Exchange has selected Avalanche ($AVAX) as the exclusive blockchain for settling tokenized U.S. stocks on its upcoming 24/7 trading platform, according to the WSJ.NYSE cited Avalanche’s speed, throughput and compliance capabilities.The platform is targeting… pic.twitter.com/uE4S3X5lnn

AVAX jumped on the news. It rose 4.3% in the minute the reports hit at 12:30 UTC, and it trades at $8.79 on Binance, up 11% on the day while Bitcoin and Ether are down.

The pick lands on a chain that holds only a small slice of the market today. Avalanche carries $179 million of the $3.73 billion in tokenized shares tracked by rwa.xyz. That is 4.8% of the market, down from 10.3% a month ago.

So can the NYSE deal make Avalanche the main home for these tokens?

The plan is not new, but the blockchain is. NYSE owner Intercontinental Exchange (ICE) first announced the platform in January and said it would seek regulatory approval.

The tokens would not be copies. ICE said they would be interchangeable with ordinary shares and carry the same dividend and voting rights.

NYSE picked Avalanche for its speed, the number of trades it can handle, and its tools for meeting regulatory rules, the Journal reported. The platform is aiming for a fourth-quarter launch, but it still needs regulators’ approval.

ICE has also signed up Securitize to issue tokenized shares for companies and funds, under a deal announced this year.

Crypto Expert Report: What Are the 10 Next Crypto to Explode in 2026?

The NYSE deal would be a big step up. We pulled the latest network breakdown from rwa.xyz, which tracks tokenized shares that investors can hold in their own wallets.

The market itself is still small next to the stock market. All the tokens it tracks add up to $3.73 billion, held by about 4.8 million wallet addresses.

The NYSE could change that scale. Every share settled through its platform would move on Avalanche, which no other chain can claim today.

There is a catch. Companies can refuse to have their shares tokenized. On OKXICE, a separate venue from OKX and ICE, 33 of the 62 companies first named had objected by late October.

Discover: JPMorgan and Coca-Cola Block Tokenized Stocks on OKXICE as Objectors Hit 33. Coinbase and Robinhood Stay Out of the List

Not yet. AVAX trades at $8.79 on Binance, up 11% from Monday’s opening price of $7.94, its best day since September 20.

The buying was heavy. In the hour that started at 12:00 UTC, about $11.8 million of AVAX changed hands on Binance. That is about 16 times a typical hour and the third-busiest hour in the past 1,000.

On the daily chart, AVAX is just below both of its exponential moving averages (EMAs), averages that weight recent prices more. The 50-day and 200-day EMAs both sit at about $9.05, so one level now does the work of two.

Crypto Expert Report: Follow The Money – Which Presales Are Attracting Crypto Whales in 2026?

For tokenized stocks, the NYSE pick is the biggest vote yet for a single chain. For AVAX, the test is whether buyers can push it above $9.05 once the initial excitement fades.

The cryptocurrency market remains under pressure, as most larger altcoins have corrected: large caps lost around 5% on average in the last 24 hours. Key levels have not been broken yet, but the overall trend is still bearish, despite yesterday's recovery.

From a technical standpoint, XRP has moved further into a downtrend, driven by more liquidations of long positions. According to the Nov. 5 snapshot, more than $12 million worth of longs has been liquidated. While the number itself is not critical, the long liquidations suggest that the asset saw an influx of buying, but it was quickly shut down.

The XRP Ledger activated the fixCleanup3_4_0 amendment on November 4 at 14:52 UTC. It removed an exploit that, under certain conditions, let accounts authorized to burn an issuer's tokens also mint them. The native supply of XRP has not been affected, luckily, so illicit actors have not used the exploit.

According to the technical analysis, the price is struggling to hold the important psychological threshold: $1.2 has already been broken, and XRP now trades at approximately $1.2.

The volume influx on the move toward the 21 EMA suggested a possible improvement in market conditions, but low volume on Friday, during the transition into the weekend trading session, disrupted any bullish plans.

As for the future, XRP is clearly moving in a longer-term downtrend; however, we will most likely see a local bounce toward $1.25. An EMA cross between the 100 EMA and the 50 EMA would simply be a signal of further price weakness and trend acceleration (most likely down).

The XRP Ledger has seen substantial growth in various on-chain metrics, which, unfortunately, does not give the price enough support. A lot of the Ledger activity appears to be automated, either trading bots or sophisticated LLM models. The market is mostly driven by speculative interest rather than fundamental network usage.

Hyperliquid fell by almost 9% on Nov. 5 and is now trading below $80, balancing on the 100 EMA, which has been broken temporarily. From a fundamental standpoint, Hyperliquid Strategies (PURR) disclosed that it has applied to become a U.S. futures commission merchant. If approved, it would be able to bring U.S. clients directly to the perpetual markets deployed on Hyperliquid.

In addition to this substantial regulatory milestone, Hyperliquid reported $620 million in quarterly net income, including $803 million in unrealized HYPE gains. Before that, on Oct. 29, Hyperliquid announced a separate ICE-Trade agreement; more details are available on the SEC's official website.

From a technical standpoint, on the daily HYPE/USDT chart, the price has bounced somewhat from a local psychological support level of approximately $77. It has been a recovery point for Hyperliquid, but, unfortunately, it is unlikely to hold if more selling pressure appears.

RSI, as a momentum indicator, is moving toward the 40 zone, so any surge of bearish pressure here could be short-lived if it is mostly speculative. However, with volume rising during the descending local trend, the bearish trend is being reinforced.

Hyperliquid (HYPE) lost its pace by the end of September, and a lower high formed in the first days of October, which is essentially the market's main signal of the end of the rally. Despite the spike at the beginning of November, it is still a lower high, which means the bearish trend is not going anywhere.

This is a relatively hard prediction to make, considering the unpredictable nature of the market. Unfortunately, the price has barely any support left, and the next support is the 200 EMA (black line on the chart), which coincides with the $68 price level.

Volume, on the other hand, is falling, which is either a normal tendency before the weekend trading session or a sign of a weakening trend for now.

Key price levels for HYPE are: $80 as the closest psychological support level, $68 as the 200 EMA, and $89 as the first psychological resistance level. The trendline resistance is at approximately $84, so a breakthrough there should become a foundation for a price recovery.

After Stellar (XLM) fell toward $0.157, there is a good chance that we are seeing accumulation or at least a transition into a sideways trend. The moving averages are not converging, which signals trend acceleration, and in this case it is a bearish one. Whenever moving averages converge, volatility is more likely to spike.

The trend on Stellar is accelerating, while volume remains relatively low and neutral.

It is no coincidence that XLM saw a trend slowdown at approximately $0.15, as it coincides with the point where the previous trend started. The death cross that occurred at the end of October is also a bearish signal.

It was followed by a spike in trading volume, which confirms the significance of the indicator and suggests that the trend may continue.

The latest network milestone for XLM is the release of Bell (Protocol 30), which was set to go live on testnet on November 3. The key change it brought to the network was post-quantum signature verification for smart contracts and millisecond ledger timestamps.

However, the mainnet validator vote, which will make the update available to users on the live network, is set to take place on November 23 at 17:00 UTC.

The bearish price performance on the market was followed by a recorded 500,000 XLM long liquidation. But considering the sheer volume of XLM on exchanges, a sub-1 million liquidation barely affects the price and will most likely have a very minor effect on the market.

From the momentum standpoint, RSI is already at a local bottom, and a further drop is possible, despite RSI already sliding to around 30. An oversold RSI is not really an issue when there is profitable capital present.

Considering the behavior of the market, there is a good chance that most of the buying support was at 1.5-1.6, so a break below the $1.5 support level could trigger a further decline, with a possible acceleration toward $1, though this is unlikely and possible only in a very bearish market.

#5331. Series A In 2026: Capital Is Flowing Faster, But Fewer Startups Are Making The Cut

More money is pouring into Series A rounds, but it isn’t opening the door to more startups. U.S. companies have raised $42 billion at that stage this year through October, up roughly 60% year over year, while deal counts remain on pace with the past few years, Crunchbase data shows.

The numbers point to an increasingly divided early-stage market. AI is fueling demand for capital and helping some startups grow at unprecedented speeds, while others struggle to turn their first customers into repeatable sales.

Investors are responding by moving in opposite directions: Some are writing much larger checks at seed to get ahead of the competition, while others are waiting until Series B or beyond for clearer evidence that a business is taking off. (At Series B, too, we’re seeing a similar trend of fewer but larger deals.)

That leaves companies still proving their growth potential navigating a Series A funding crunch even as capital floods into the fastest-growing businesses.

The low point for Series A funding in the past five years was 2023, with $23 billion invested in U.S.-based startups. Series A investment totals each year since have grown, doubling this year compared to 2023.

At the same time, round counts have settled, averaging 1,200 companies funded at Series A at $1 million or more in 2023 through 2025. This year, the trend is holding, with round counts in that range, give or take 100 deals.

“On the application side, it’s a bit harder, and that’s where I think there’s more of a Series A crunch,” according to Siddharth Ramakrishnan, a partner at Scale Venture Partners, which primarily leads Series A and B rounds.

This dynamic — steady deal count despite much more money flowing — is also impacting how early-stage VCs invest.

Among investors, there’s more competition, especially at the early stage. In turn, VCs are increasingly pursuing one of two opposing strategies: either writing much larger checks much earlier, or holding back until later rounds, Ramakrishnan said.

With the first strategy, check sizes are getting much bigger, he noted, with $10 million to $20 million seed deals not uncommon. “Instead of waiting till the Series A, where they have $4 million in revenue and growing, you’re going to do it when they have $500,000 in revenue, they have a pilot, the team is smart,” he said.

Other investors are waiting to invest later. “ ‘I’m not getting any new information by the time they’re at $2 million in revenue from $500,000, so I’m just going to wait until they actually take off,’ and then you’re seeing a gap,” Ramakrishnan said, explaining the thinking behind this investment approach. “People are putting in a lot of money at the Series B, Series C onwards, because that’s when you get the signal that things are really working.”

Scale expects there to be a bit more variance in this current fund. Its preference is to stay at Series A and B risk profile, by “potentially pulling a little bit earlier and a little bit later and recreating it in the aggregate,” he said.

The firm’s most recent fund 8 is its largest to date at $900 million, up from its prior $600 million fund.

“We still think that Series A is a great place to be if you can make it happen, because it’s at that point where you ideally have enough information to make an informed bet, but not enough that there’s still some of the growth investors that are scared to come in,” Ramakrishnan said, “and so you get great companies at great prices.”

At each quartile, U.S. Series A rounds have trended up in size this year, Crunchbase data shows. So far in 2026, 10% of Series A rounds are $75 million and over, up from $50 million in 2025.

Those much-larger checks are translating into hypergrowth for some companies. “Instead of going zero to $7 million, which in the old world would have been amazing numbers, now there’s people going zero to $20 million, or zero to $30 million,” Ramakrishnan said.

For founders, securing those larger checks often hinges on turning a handful of early customers into a repeatable sales process. Many startups get stuck in that transition, even as investors compete to back those that break through.

“If you have the ambition to build a world-class company, then you also need to raise a big Series A to expand and go abroad, take on different types of markets,” according to European seed investor Anke Huiskes of NP-Hard Ventures, whom I interviewed on-stage at the HumanX Amsterdam conference on AI earlier this year.

“I think the whole messy phase is in this go-to-market phase where you don’t really know who your ideal customer profile is,” said Huiskes, who invests at the seed stage in product-focused founders.

She’s seen startups get stuck when they have a few customers but aren’t growing fast enough. “A lot of the companies hang out here,” she said.

But for the companies who build that repetitive sales cycle, VCs are eagerly reaching out, she said: “And then I get a text, ‘Can you please give me an intro?’ And all of a sudden, I have 10 term sheets. So it’s really black and white.”

#5327. Startup Founders Are Using AI To File Patents. Here’s Where DIY Becomes A Liability.

Patents can help startups establish competitive advantage, attract investors and protect innovations. But the traditional patent process is expensive, slow and difficult to navigate, particularly for companies with limited resources.

AI is changing that equation. General-purpose tools can research existing patents, document inventions and generate drafts that look like patent applications in minutes. Handling the process themselves can seem like an easy way for founders to save money.

But AI’s capabilities are jagged. AI can perform some tasks remarkably well while missing legal and strategic issues that determine a patent’s commercial value. An application can look sophisticated while providing little meaningful protection.

For example, a patent’s claims define its legal boundaries and what you can stop competitors from doing. Mistakes involving claim scope may remain hidden until an investor, acquirer or competitor scrutinizes the company’s intellectual property.

The question isn’t whether startups should use AI. It’s how much founders can safely do themselves and when legal expertise becomes essential.

Founders can use AI to organize technical documentation, summarize existing patents and identify potentially relevant prior art. Turning engineering notes into an organized invention disclosure, for example, can reduce preparation costs and help counsel focus on strategy.

But the opportunity extends beyond DIY. The right counsel can orchestrate AI across the workflow, coordinating invention discovery, drafting, drawings and quality checks. AI can help counsel explore alternative implementations with the inventors, identify disclosure gaps and check support for claims. Attorneys can direct that work, evaluate the results and connect each step to best protect business needs.

That combination can produce more comprehensive applications with substantially greater efficiency. It is fundamentally different from generating an application with a chatbot and asking a lawyer to review it afterward.

The cheapest filing option is not necessarily the most economical. A poorly prepared application can create false confidence while leaving valuable innovations exposed.

Counsel can help decide what to patent versus maintain as a trade secret, prioritize filings within the company’s budget and assess deadlines before disclosure or filing limits the available options. An internal process that competitors cannot observe or reverse engineer, for example, may be better kept as a trade secret.

Claim scope requires particular judgment. A fraud detection claim tied to one algorithm may leave competitors free to deliver the same functionality using another. Overly broad claims may overlap with existing technology. Valuable claims target what competitors must do to compete. Ideally, a single identifiable competitor can infringe them, and that infringement can be detected and proven.

The specification must describe alternatives and variations that support broader claims later without unnecessarily limiting their scope. AI can assist, but strategic judgment must guide the work.

Filing volume says little about commercial value. Investors and acquirers will look beyond the number of pending applications to ask:

AI’s greatest value is not simply generating more applications at lower costs. It is making meaningful protection more accessible without sacrificing legal judgment.

Founders should ask how a firm coordinates its AI tools and legal expertise, not simply whether it uses AI. The answer should explain how that process improves both efficiency and substance.

Ultimately, the most expensive patent mistake may be discovering too late that a DIY application never adequately protected the innovation on which the business was built.

Michael Drapkin is a founding partner of Landfall IP, an AI-native patent law firm based in Boulder, Colorado. He previously founded one of the largest electronics and computer patent prosecution practices in the U.S. at an Am Law 100 firm and was named U.S. Patent Practitioner of the Year by Managing IP in 2022.

Nathan Mutter is managing partner and founder of Landfall IP, an AI-Native law firm. He has served as top outside counsel at Oura, Coinbase, Rubrik, Salesforce 1 and many others. #5326. Loopscale Pauses Protocol After kySOL Collateral Was Priced as zBTC in a 4,597 SOL Loan

AI-assisted summary, reviewed by NullTX editors.

Loopscale's Genesis Vault lent 4,597 SOL against a single kySOL token that the protocol valued as ten zBTC. The decimal mismatch behind it is the most instructive part of the incident, and a second attack path shows how far the probing went.

One token worth roughly $120 was all a Loopscale vault held when it handed out 4,597 SOL, because the protocol read that token as ten Bitcoin-denominated coins. The arithmetic behind the mistake is simple.

Loopscale, a Solana lending protocol built around Genesis Vaults, paused operations on November 5 after a week of what it called a sustained campaign by a sophisticated actor. Its APIs were taking more than 30,000 malicious requests a day. Loopscale's pause announcement, as summarized on CoinMarketCap, says user deposits remain secure and affected vaults were restored. The team has not named the suspected attacker.

The loan itself can be traced onchain. A November 1 transaction shows a wallet Loopscale identified drawing 4,597 SOL after depositing one kySOL, a restaked SOL token. The collateral deposit paired kySOL with a zBTC asset identifier, which backs up Loopscale's account that the collateral was valued as a different asset.

An independent researcher's trace found that the attacker bought one kySOL for about 1.31 SOL and deposited it into Loopscale roughly 154 seconds later. The protocol priced it as ten zBTC. At the loan's implied SOL price, that kySOL was worth somewhere near $120, while ten zBTC would be worth about ten Bitcoin.

The numbers line up with a decimal mismatch. On Solana, each token's mint account stores its own decimal precision, as Solana's documentation on tokens explains. kySOL uses nine decimals, like SOL, while a Bitcoin-denominated token such as zBTC uses eight. One kySOL is 1,000,000,000 base units, and read at eight decimals, that same raw balance comes out to 10.0. The protocol never had to be fooled about the price of Bitcoin. It only had to read one token's raw amount on another token's decimal scale.

That arithmetic explains the reported valuation, but it is not a root-cause statement from Loopscale. The team's own description is broader: a misconfigured combination of asset-pricing parameters caused collateral to be valued as a different asset. The result was an undercollateralized loan of about $412,000.

The harder question is how the protocol accepted a mismatch at all. According to the researcher's analysis, the attacker picked a price entry for zBTC, labeled the collateral as an Orca position and deposited kySOL. Under the Orca collateral rule, the kySOL mint was allowed to differ from the zBTC identifier. Labeling it as a standard SPL token would have failed, since that rule demands the mint and identifier match.

That detail matters more than the decimals. Each rule looked sensible by itself, and the flaw lived in the combination: a price source, a collateral type label and a mint check that together let one token be priced as another. It also explains why Loopscale pointed to both its publicly inspectable program logic and its private transaction-building APIs. Thirty thousand requests a day reads like systematic probing for a combination the normal API would build or authorize.

Loopscale's November 6 update named two attack paths. The second went after the USDC Genesis Vault. Per the protocol, an atomic transaction bundle sold a loan carrying an extreme interest rate into the vault, inflating its net asset value and setting up a disproportionate redemption of about $521,000. Loopscale says its systems halted that redemption within 30 seconds of the transaction being generated.

So the incident ended in two different outcomes. The SOL path produced a real undercollateralized loan, while the USDC path was an attempt the team says it stopped. Counting both as stolen would overstate the damage, and Loopscale maintains that depositors took no loss and that affected vaults were made whole.

Loopscale linked four addresses in its disclosure. The two Solana addresses are 247Lk5YNH9URfBBvxVUtDruz8GvGX8gKGuYHVCZThpiR and AzPh2dUV3duK9n8PWV6CxKMwWr9Rk7fxPNBZuv1CiwMr.

The two EVM addresses are 0xb8959Aca4e4C796A3BaDA66833eAe60b1BC0bfb2 and 0xB7Ec7eF24FD73f3000C651CA9D0Fa45b61DcF854. Reports indicate the borrowed SOL was bridged out of the protocol, which fits the pairing of Solana and EVM addresses.

The loan's later history is visible onchain as well. A November 3 liquidation of the same loan moved about 4,598.4 SOL from a separate wallet back to the lending strategy. The researcher's trace puts the figure at 4,598.434180621 wSOL against 4,597 SOL borrowed, a gap of roughly 1.43 SOL. The liquidator received the lone kySOL as collateral. The public record doesn't yet show who funded that liquidation, so Loopscale's post-mortem will need to explain how the vault was made whole.

The takeaways are narrow and practical. Decimal scales should come from the token's own mint data rather than a configured identifier, and a deposit should fail when the collateral's mint doesn't match the asset the pricing path assumes. Private transaction-building APIs deserve the same scrutiny as onchain code, because an attacker who can probe them tens of thousands of times a day can map out which combinations they will build.

Vault accounting needs limits too. An extreme interest rate that is legal in the program can still reprice a share if the vault treats the loan mark as authoritative, which is why the 30-second halt on the second path counted for so much.

This looks less like a clever exploit than a missing sanity check. A deposit worth about $120 should never support a 4,597 SOL loan, and a simple ceiling on collateral value against the borrower's deposited units would have flagged it. Loopscale also lost $5.8 million in April 2025 to a pricing flaw before recovering the funds, so the next thing to watch is whether its post-mortem shows pricing safeguards that match how often this class of bug has shown up.

#5320. Bitcoin vs Gold: History Points to a Potential BTC Comeback in 2027

As of Tuesday, November 10, the Bitcoin vs gold race has an unusual score for 2026: both are losing. Bitcoin (BTC) is down 15.1% this year, and gold is down 5.9%.

That is rare. We compared the two assets’ returns up to November 10 in every year since 2015. Both were down at this point only twice before, in 2018 and 2022.

Gold is still ahead on the year. Gold futures trade at $4,086 an ounce, 23% below their record close of $5,318 on January 29. Bitcoin, at $74,259, is 40.5% below its record close of $124,753 from October 2025.

The calendar favors gold too. In each of the past 11 years, whichever asset led on November 10 also finished the year ahead.

But 2018 and 2022 ended the same way: Bitcoin hit its cycle low within six weeks and then beat gold by a wide margin the next year. So is 2026 setting up the same turn for 2027?

The two earlier cases point the same way, though two cases are a small sample to build on.

Both rebounds came in the year before a Bitcoin halving, the event every four years that cuts the number of new coins miners receive by half. The halvings fell in 2020 and 2024, and the next one is expected in 2028. That puts 2027 in the same slot as 2019 and 2023.

This year itself looks settled. Bitcoin beat gold in 8 of the 11 full years since 2015, and gold won only in 2018, 2022 and 2025. In every one of those 11 years, the asset that led on November 10 stayed ahead to December 31. Gold leads by about nine percentage points, so history hands it 2026, its second win in a row.

Crypto Expert Report: What Are the 10 Next Crypto to Explode in 2026?

Gold’s slide has been steep for a metal. It closed at a record $5,318 on January 29, fell as low as $3,899 on October 30, and now trades at $4,086.

Investors have not walked away. Gold exchange-traded funds (ETFs) hold physical gold and trade like stocks. Worldwide, they added $2.7 billion in October, their fourth straight month of inflows, the World Gold Council reported on November 5. Their holdings rose 19 tonnes to a record 4,275 tonnes. Over the first ten months of the year, the funds took in $41 billion, the third-strongest run on record. North American funds were the exception, with small outflows.

Bitcoin has done better since February. Measured in gold, one Bitcoin bought 21.1 ounces on January 5. By February 23, that had fallen to 12.4 ounces, the lowest since March 2023. It now buys 18.2 ounces.

The gap since that February low is wide. Bitcoin is up 14.9% since February 23, while gold is down 21.8%. Since June 30, Bitcoin has gained 26.8% and gold 1.2%.

Both assets face the same test today. The U.S. Bureau of Labor Statistics publishes October’s consumer price index (CPI), the main measure of inflation, at 8:30 a.m. in New York, or 13:30 UTC.

Bitcoin trades at $74,278 ahead of the release. On Sunday, it fell to $73,510, its lowest price since August 21.

On the daily chart, where each candle covers one day, Bitcoin sits below both of its exponential moving averages (EMAs), averages that give recent prices more weight. The 200-day EMA stands at $76,480 and the 50-day EMA at $79,124.

For gold, the line to watch is $3,899, the October 30 low. In the Bitcoin vs gold race, gold is on track to take 2026. If Bitcoin holds $73,510 and its 2018 and 2022 pattern repeats, 2027 is the year history gives to Bitcoin.

#5319. Anthropic Seeks Record $88.5B Tied To Public Market Debut

Anthropic is seeking to secure up to $88.5 billion in its planned IPO and a concurrent private placement, potentially making it the largest-ever fundraise tied to a public market debut.

On Tuesday, the AI giant submitted an updated S-1 filing for its upcoming public offering, unveiling new details including a proposed share price range offering size. The offering could set a fully diluted valuation of up to $1.4 trillion for the San Francisco company.

Anthropic’s expected valuation comes in below earlier projections, with many investors reportedly forecasting something closer to $2 trillion. That said, even at $1.4 trillion, Anthropic would still be going public at the second-highest valuation in history, topped only by SpaceX’s June debut.

The offering should also provide Anthropic with plentiful capital to pursue its expensive expansion and infrastructure investment plans.

For the IPO portion of its fundraise, Anthropic plans to sell just over 800 million shares 1 at $70 to $78 each. At the high end, that would bring in around $62.5 billion — the largest ever IPO fundraise after SpaceX’s $75 billion offering.

Anthropic also expects to pull in another $26 billion from a private placement slated to close immediately following the IPO. Investors in this include AMD, Broadcom, Google, Micron Technology, Microsoft, Nvidia and TSMC.

Put together, it’s a record-setting capital haul for a company making its market debut, which Anthropic is expected to do later this month on Nasdaq under the ticker symbol ANT.

Anthropic also recently updated its financial disclosures, showing results through September of this year.

For the first nine months of the year, the company had $33.2 billion in revenue, up from $2.5 billion in the same period a year ago. It’s an astounding growth rate, albeit Anthropic is already known for this.

The company claims it has the fastest enterprise adoption of any technology in history, growing revenue from zero at commercial launch in the first quarter of 2023 to $17 billion for the three months ended Sept. 30, 2026.

As of yet, however, it’s not profitable. Anthropic posted an operating loss of $1.3 billion for the first nine months of the year, down from $5.2 billion a year earlier. Its net loss widened to $104 billion, up from $25.1 billion a year ago.

The total offering is for 825 million shares, of which 23.6 million will be from selling shareholders.↩

It reserves a share of each block's gas capacity for eligible payments, protecting that capacity from general traffic. The default reservation is 5% of each block's gas limit.

Payment Lane sets aside capacity for qualifying BNB transfers between wallets, so unrelated activity cannot use it all. Token payments can also qualify once approved for the lane.

Ripple contributed to a white paper commissioned by the Dubai Financial Services Authority (DFSA), which brings together perspectives and  insights from leading practitioners across the financial services ecosystem.

Ripple's Managing Director, Middle East & Africa, Reece Merrick, recently stated his contribution to  the DFSA's new publication: "Scaling Tokenization: The Road Ahead," alongside leaders from BlackRock, Standard Chartered and Robinhood.

The white paper considers the conditions that may support the responsible scaling of tokenised financial assets and related market infrastructure, including within the Dubai International Financial Centre (DIFC).

Aside from Merrick, other contributors include Tony Ashraf, Managing Director, Head of Technology & Operations and Head of Digital Assets, Middle East & Africa at BlackRock; Coy Garrison, Senior Director and Deputy General Counsel, Crypto at Robinhood; René Michau, Global Head, Digital Asset Advisory at Standard Chartered;  Henson Orser, Founder and Chief  Executive at Soter Insure; and Herman Schueller, Director, Innovation and Technology Risk Supervision at DFSA.

According to the DFSA report, tokenization of traditional financial assets has the potential to become a significant development in mainstream financial markets, offering the prospect of greater access for investors, increased efficiency for issuers and intermediaries, and reduced risk in certain areas, especially around settlement, for the wider financial system.

Merrick shared his perspective, saying that the real shift is not just tokenized treasuries and MMFs (Money Market Funds) gaining AUM but rather their on-chain utility as collateral in repo and margin without needing to redeem to cash first. This viewpoint follows as repo markets continue to move trillions daily, with Merrick highlighting this as potential for tokenization.

Merrick anticipates massive growth in this regard over the next 12 months, predicting that a significant proportion of that will be on the XRP Ledger.

"With clear frameworks, institutional custody, and trusted settlement assets like RLUSD, the UAE, DIFC and Ripple are positioned at the forefront of this next phase," Merrick stated.

Forecasts for the future size of tokenised assets vary considerably. Citi Institute's base case is for the global market in tokenised financial assets to reach $5.5 trillion by 2030.  A Standard Chartered and Synpulse paper estimated that demand for tokenised assets could reach $30.1 trillion by 2034.

#5314. FinCEN Bars US Institutions From Transmitting Funds to MEXC: What Changes and What Doesn't

AI-assisted summary, reviewed by NullTX editors.

FinCEN's November 6 order cuts US financial institutions off from MEXC Global, barring any transmittal of funds to or from the exchange. The order spells out what is banned, what MEXC is accused of, and how the exchange has answered.

MEXC says user assets remain secure. The FinCEN order never suggested otherwise, and the gap between the exchange's reassurance and the order's actual target is the key to this story.

On November 6, the Financial Crimes Enforcement Network issued a final order under Section 9714(a) of the Combating Russian Money Laundering Act. It names MEXC Global a financial institution of primary money laundering concern in connection with Russian illicit finance. From there, it bars "covered financial institutions," a category that includes banks, broker-dealers and money transmitters, from any transmittal of funds to or from MEXC Global. Transmittals, as defined, include convertible virtual currency.

On the MEXC side, the reach is wide. The order covers the exchange's subsidiaries, branches and offices outside the United States: MEXC Global Ltd and MX Global Ltd in Seychelles, MEXC Estonia OÜ, GIDA Technology AG in Switzerland and MXC Global Ltd in the United Kingdom. Former Singapore entities and any successors are included as well. US-based affiliates, by contrast, are expressly excluded.

The ban won't bite right away. It takes effect 30 days after publication in the Federal Register, which had not happened as of the announcement, and it carries no end date. FinCEN keeps the authority to attach conditions and grant exemptions, and willful violations can lead to civil and criminal penalties under 31 U.S.C. 5321 and 5322.

MEXC's statement is short and carefully built. The exchange says it is aware of the order and is reviewing it with its legal and compliance teams. It describes itself as operating normally, with user assets secure. It also says it takes the concerns seriously, plans to engage constructively with FinCEN and other regulators, and has started an independent review of its AML and sanctions controls.

Two points stand out. For one, the reassurance lines up with the order's text. Nothing in it freezes balances or halts trading, so "operating normally" is plausible. The threat is to MEXC's access to US financial counterparties, not to the exchange's wallets.

The other point is what the statement skips. It disputes none of the allegations, and the independent review it promises targets AML and sanctions controls, the very area where FinCEN says the exchange failed. The order also invites anyone with relevant information to submit it to FinCEN, so MEXC already has a formal channel for the constructive engagement it describes.

The charges are specific. FinCEN assesses that MEXC facilitated at least $16.7 billion in likely illicit activity between May 2021 and May 2026, a figure Treasury's announcement rounded to $16 billion. The order splits that total across several categories.

On Russia, FinCEN cites nearly $1.5 billion in direct and indirect exposure to sanctions-evasion transactions, including $232 million in direct dealings with entities sanctioned by the US, EU or UK. According to the order, MEXC processed about $129 million with Garantex and $4.1 million with its successor Grinex after both were designated, with activity continuing as recently as June 2026. It also points to at least $26 million benefiting the A7 Network and nearly $200 million tied to the ruble-backed A7A5 token. Beyond that, FinCEN says MEXC handled more than $13 billion with four UK-sanctioned exchanges between May 2018 and July 2026.

Iran features just as heavily. The order cites nearly $2 billion tied to Iranian actors or terrorist groups, including about $1.87 billion in exposure to Iran and over $1 billion in direct transactions with more than 40 Iranian exchanges. About $22 million is linked to the Central Bank of Iran and the IRGC Quds Force. For North Korea, the order describes roughly $350,000 received by a sanctioned money launderer between June and September 2025. On cybercrime, it cites $1.99 billion in flows linked to illicit cyber actors and $37.9 million in suspected ransomware payments between January 2022 and July 2024.

The order then turns to MEXC's own rulebook. Its stated KYC and AML policies prohibit accounts in certain jurisdictions, yet FinCEN says the exchange facilitated transactions involving them. The order also notes that MEXC has operated without a license in Seychelles, Hong Kong and Japan, and it points to the Seychelles Financial Services Authority's May 2026 enforcement action against MX Global Ltd. All of this reflects FinCEN's assessments, drawn from public and non-public information, and MEXC has not answered them point by point.

The order is not an OFAC sanctions designation, and the difference matters. A funds-transmittal ban limits what US-covered institutions can do with MEXC. It does not make it illegal for ordinary users anywhere in the world to hold an account there. The order also states that it leaves existing Bank Secrecy Act and OFAC obligations untouched.

Section 9714 gives Treasury two routes: the special measures of Section 311 of the USA PATRIOT Act, or a ban on certain transmittals of funds. FinCEN took the second and explained its reasoning. Recordkeeping requirements would still let transfers continue, and a correspondent-account restriction would miss funds moving outside a strict correspondent relationship. FinCEN also went with an order rather than a rulemaking, citing imminent threats and ongoing transactions.

One provision stands out for its practicality. FinCEN acknowledges that a covered institution often can't reject incoming crypto before it arrives, so the order allows discretion in cases such as funds that sat in an unhosted wallet for an extended period. The carve-out underlines how difficult enforcement will be in practice.

For most MEXC customers outside the US, nothing changes on day one. Counterparties face a tougher picture. Once the order takes effect, US banks, regulated exchanges and money transmitters will have to block transmittals to and from MEXC, and global institutions with US exposure have strong reasons to follow suit. FinCEN says plainly that the order puts US and foreign financial institutions and regulators on notice.

Before issuance, the draft went to the Justice Department, State, the Federal Reserve, the FDIC, the SEC, the CFTC, the OCC and the NCUA, and none objected. The order also fits into a wider Treasury campaign. It cites the October 1 Operation Economic Outcast action against the A7 Network, and a separate FinCEN proposal on A7 sub-agents followed days later.

Predicting how users or markets will react would be guesswork. What users can do is track the dates, know which institutions they depend on, and watch for official updates from MEXC.

FinCEN used the same Section 9714 authority against the exchange Bitzlato in January 2023. This time, though, the target is by FinCEN's own account among the 20 largest exchanges by trading volume, with roughly 9% of centralized exchange market share as of December 2025 and about $5 billion in reserve assets as of June 2026. Applying a transmittal ban to an exchange of that size signals a more aggressive posture.

Three things will show what comes next. The first is the Federal Register publication date, which starts the 30-day clock. The second is whether FinCEN grants any exemptions or conditions. The third is what MEXC's independent review turns up, and whether the exchange shares the results. For now, the statement buys MEXC time without answering the order. The real answer will come from changes to its controls, and from whether its banking and liquidity partners are satisfied with them.

#5313. NVIDIA Tokenized Stocks Priced Monday’s Drop 18 Hours Before Wall Street Opened. Earnings Next?

NVIDIA tokenized stocks traded through a shock on Sunday, November 8, when news about Nvidia’s CEO broke while Wall Street was closed. At 20:12 UTC, CNBC reported that Nvidia’s board was investigating CEO Jensen Huang’s relationship with a woman U.S. intelligence agencies suspect of spying for China.

The stock market was closed. Tokenized versions of Nvidia, which trade around the clock on crypto platforms, were not. Within 30 minutes, Nvidia’s market on Hyperliquid fell 3.3%.

By the time Wall Street opened on Monday, 18 hours later, the token traders had already found the price. Hyperliquid’s Nvidia market stood at $173.27 a minute before the opening bell. Nvidia opened at $173.07, just 0.1% away.

Nvidia reports earnings on November 17, after the market closes. So can tokenized stocks call the move again?

The weekend gave tokenized markets a clean test. Nvidia closed Friday at $186.64 on the Nasdaq, and nothing traded on Wall Street until pre-market trading opened at 4 a.m. in New York on Monday, or 09:00 UTC.

We tracked Nvidia’s price on Hyperliquid minute by minute. The market there is a perpetual contract run by trade.xyz, a type of futures contract with no expiry date that follows the share price.

Backed tokens moved the same way. NVIDIA xStock (NVDAx), a token on Solana backed by real Nvidia shares, fell from $188.13 on Sunday at 20:00 UTC to $175.98 by 08:00 UTC on Monday. Hourly prices on CoinGecko show the same overnight slide.

Crypto Expert Report: What is the Best Meme Coin to Buy and Forget Until the Next Bullrun?

The news pulled in traders. Between Friday’s close and Monday’s pre-market, $258.5 million worth of Nvidia traded on Hyperliquid.

That is 4.7 times the average of the four weekends before, when the same 60-hour window saw $33 million to $72 million.

The timing explains it. Over a normal weekend, almost nothing happens to Nvidia, so the tokenized market is quiet. This weekend, it was one of the few places where traders could act on the news for about 13 hours.

There is an irony here. On November 2, Nvidia joined the companies objecting to tokenized versions of their shares on OKXICE, the planned venue from NYSE owner Intercontinental Exchange (ICE) and the crypto exchange OKX.

Discover: JPMorgan and Coca-Cola Block Tokenized Stocks on OKXICE as Objectors Hit 33. Coinbase and Robinhood Stay Out of the List

The next big Nvidia news will also land when Wall Street is mostly closed. Nvidia reports its third-quarter results on Tuesday, November 17, after the market closes, with a call at 5 p.m. in New York.

The regular after-hours session runs until 8 p.m. in New York. From then until 4 a.m., tokenized markets are among the few places still trading Nvidia.

The test will be harder this time. Weekend news hit a quiet market with one clear direction. Earnings bring a flood of numbers at once, and the first move after a report often reverses.

Nvidia trades at $173.17 on the Nasdaq on Tuesday, down 3.1% after hotter-than-expected U.S. inflation data. It touched $170.12, its lowest price since March 31. It is 28% below its record close of $239.24 on October 6.

On Hyperliquid’s four-hour chart, where each candle covers four hours, Nvidia sits below both of its exponential moving averages (EMAs), averages that give recent prices more weight. The 50-period EMA stands at $189.53 and the 200-period EMA at $206.78.

Crypto Expert Report: What Are the 10 Next Crypto to Explode in 2026?

For NVIDIA tokenized stocks, the weekend was proof that they can price news before Wall Street. On November 17, watch the tokenized price between 8 p.m. and 4 a.m. in New York for the first read on Nvidia’s earnings.

Dogecoin community member Mishaboar has raised concerns about the security risks associated with social signing, a feature that allows users to create and access a blockchain wallet using everyday accounts like Google, Apple ID, Telegram, or email instead of managing a complex seed phrase.

This comes after Keplr, a multichain wallet supporting Cosmos, Bitcoin, Ethereum, and Starknet, stated it had received reports of unauthorized transactions on some Keplr accounts created with Google or Apple login.

The wallet provider stated that the incident has been escalated to the Web3Auth team, with both working together to investigate the matter.

Before Keplr's disclosure, Web3 wallet infrastructure provider Web3Auth said it was aware of a security issue affecting Web3Auth's services used by some third parties. It stated that it had temporarily paused the embedded wallet service in response to the issue; however, after an initial investigation, no evidence was found that MetaMask users were impacted.

In his X post, Mishaboar criticized social signing. "Social signing, the feature you may want to add to your wallet if you hate your users," Mishaboar wrote.

Social signing, the feature you may want to add to your wallet if you hate your users. The worst part is that the users that use the social signing option -and which will end up being hacked through it - are also often newbies, entering crypto for the first time. And the risk goes beyond the funds in your wallet - data leaks could link your real life identity to your holdings, which can have terrible consequences.

The concern is particularly significant for inexperienced crypto users who may not recognize the risks associated with connecting their personal accounts to wallet services. While the feature makes wallet creation and access easier, it could introduce security vulnerabilities that users may not fully understand, Mishaboar argued.

"The worst part is that the users that use the social signing option—and who will end up being hacked through it—are also often newbies, entering crypto for the first time. And the risk goes beyond the funds in your wallet—data leaks could link your real-life identity to your holdings, which can have terrible consequences," Mishaboar stated.

Mishaboar noted that this warning also extends to wallets using social sign-in, which allows users to back up their keys in the "Cloud," which just means somebody else's server, he explained.

This week, a security advisory was issued for iOS users, who are urged to update their devices to enhance their wallet security. This follows security researchers identifying two exploit kits, Coruna and DarkSword, which target devices running older iOS versions. These do not rely on a flaw in any wallet app, but once a device is compromised, they can access wallet data stored on it.

#5311. Ukraine’s new pocket-sized gadget turns Russian drones’ cameras against them

Ukrainian drone teams have a new way to spy on the drones that spy on them. A Kyiv equipment startup called CODE380 has been gaining attention for a pocket-sized receiver, the D·Vision SDR, that picks up live camera video from many Russian drones and shows it on a screen.

Those drones send their video over the air without any scrambling, so anyone with the right receiver can watch along. A Ukrainian unit can see where a drone is heading and what its pilot is aiming at before it hits.

According to Defense News, the device is light, at about 10 ounces, which is less than half the weight of competing Ukrainian models, one of which weighs a couple of pounds.

It also listens on the radio channels Russia’s newer Molniya drones started using for video in June. Serhii “Flash” Beskrestnov, a radio specialist who advises Ukraine’s president, said in a June Facebook post cited by Defense News that “most detectors don’t see these frequencies, or see them poorly.” He warned that putting too much trust in a detector could prove fatal.

Beskrestnov has also warned that digital video could one day replace analog, which would blind receivers like this one. The New York Times reported in August that some Molniyas are AI-guided, using Nvidia chips and emitting no signals.

The immediate resistance level is at $1.20. Breaking above it will be a clear indicator of an uptrend.

#5308. The TechCrunch Founder Summit agenda is only half the reason to be in Boston on November 4

You can learn a lot from a great founder session. But sometimes the conversation that changes what you do next happens five minutes after the session ends. And with the event happening tomorrow, there is another reason to make sure you are in the room: The format is designed to help founders learn in different ways throughout the day.

On November 4, TechCrunch Founder Summit 2026 brings founders and investors together at SoWa Power Station in Boston for one day of practical learning, candid conversations, live pitching, smaller roundtables, and networking.

Register now to save up to $100 on your pass, plus get a second for free. Or save up to 30% on group bundles.

The Build Stage focuses on the decisions founders make while they are still shaping, testing, and growing the business. These sessions get into the mechanics behind building a company, from distribution and fundraising to team building and pitching.

Hunter Worland of NEA opens the conversation on why distribution can become a startup’s next competitive advantage, especially when strong technology alone is not enough to win customers.

Kristen Craft of Fidelity Private Shares brings a current view of fundraising trends, helping founders understand how the capital environment is shifting and what that means for the way they approach their next raise.

The stage also gets tactical about building high-performing teams and sharpening the story you tell investors, customers, and potential hires.

Dave Balter of True Ventures and Edisyl takes on a deceptively simple question: Does your pitch earn the next conversation?

The value of the Build Stage is straightforward: These are lessons founders can take back to their companies immediately.

If the Build Stage is about creating momentum, the Impact Stage is about what happens once that momentum becomes real. This is where founders can step back and think about bigger decisions around product-market fit, scaling, enterprise relationships, leadership, and long-term growth.

Steve Fredette, president, co-founder, and director of Toast, brings the perspective of building and scaling one of Boston’s most recognizable startup success stories.

Rudina Seseri, founder and managing partner of Glasswing Ventures, explores the tension every founder eventually faces: when to scale and when hitting the brakes may actually protect the business.

Kent Bennett of Bessemer Venture Partners tackles product-market fit before scale, helping founders think more critically about whether the signals they are seeing truly justify the next phase of growth.

Chase Garbarino, CEO and co-founder of HqO, brings the conversation home with the Boston Founder Playbook and a perspective on building ambitious companies outside the Bay Area.

The Impact Stage is valuable because it creates space for founders to get out of the weeds for a moment and ask whether they are scaling the right things, in the right way, at the right time.

Main Stage sessions can give you perspective. Roundtables give you room to get specific.

Founder Summit’s smaller roundtables are built around highly focused problems that many founders are actively solving right now, from entering difficult verticals and building enterprise trust to creating lean teams and opening doors with major customers.

Chirag Shah of Define Ventures digs into what happens when your first vertical is also one of the hardest to enter.

A technical session with Shishir Tewari of Procore Technologies moves the AI conversation from broad hype to the practical challenge of reducing hallucinations with better enterprise context.

Merve Kitapci of ADIN.AI gets highly specific about enterprise selling and what it takes to land major global customers before Series A.

Andy Tang of Draper Associates opens a different kind of founder conversation: What if you are building something the market does not even have a name for yet?

Linden Tibbets of IFTTT explores how AI may change the assumptions founders make about team size, productivity, and what a smaller company can realistically accomplish.

The value here is participation. Instead of simply hearing how someone else approached a problem, founders can bring their own questions, compare experiences with the people around the table, and leave with ideas that are much closer to their actual business.

Founder Summit also gives attendees the chance to see what happens when founders put their stories in front of investors in real time.

During “So You Think You Can Pitch?,” founders make their cases in front of investors, including Dave Balter, Chirag Shah, and Simran Suri of Maveron.

This is one of the most interactive parts of the day because it turns advice about pitching into something founders can actually watch: what gets an investor’s attention, where a story loses momentum, and which questions come up immediately.

For anyone preparing to raise, sell, recruit, or simply explain their company more clearly, seeing those reactions live can be incredibly useful.

Schedule a one-on-one conversation. Join a small group. Find someone who wants to talk about the exact challenge you are working through.

The day wraps up with a closing reception presented by Fidelity Private Shares, giving attendees time to keep the conversations going without rushing to the next session.

That matters because some of the most useful connections at an event happen after you have already shared a room, a question, or a conversation earlier in the day.

The Impact Stage creates room for bigger growth and leadership decisions. The roundtables let you ask questions and go deeper. The live pitch competition puts founder storytelling to the test. Macro conditions also amplify this trend: elevated global debt levels, persistent fiscal dominance, and periodic currency instability drive a widespread flight into hard assets. SHIB futures flows are down 67x, suggesting futures traders are pulling back on SHIB exposure in a big way, rather than holding or adding leveraged exposure. Such a move can be a sign of weaker speculative interest, profit-taking, or traders exiting positions in unclear market conditions.

Futures flow measures activity in the derivatives market, not demand for SHIB in the spot market. The big drop could be an indication that traders are moving away from leveraged bets, partly due to the uncertainty in the markets right now.

SHIB's price impact will partly depend on whether spot market demand can offset the fall in futures flow. If buyers keep buying tokens and selling pressure is kept at bay, this might not have much impact on SHIB's price.

#5305. Rivian spinout Also was working on an e-moto project in Kenya — until it walked away

Also, the micromobility startup spun out of Rivian in 2025, quietly started and then walked away from an electric two-wheeler pilot project in Kenya earlier this year, as it sought to focus its resources on its consumer e-bike and autonomous vehicle ambitions, TechCrunch has learned.

The project received grant funding from the Shell Foundation, an independent charity established by the British oil and gas giant Shell plc. A section of the Shell Foundation’s website that has since been removed said the project’s goal was to “enable and de-risk global OEM entry into Africa’s EV market by piloting a locally integrated electric two-wheeler platform in Kenya, with potential to scale across East Africa.”

According to the deleted section, Also was expected to work on modular battery designs and distributed EV charging, and planned on “developing a purpose-built electric motorcycle for African riders.”

The opportunity for electric motorcycles seems ripe on the continent, which has a massive two-wheeler market. African mobility company Spiro recently said it has more than 130,000 electric motorcycles operating across seven countries, along with 2,500 battery-swapping stations. This boom has drawn interest from Chinese mobility companies and investors, which are pouring resources into the space.

In a September email, Also told TechCrunch that it had “explored this project” with an unnamed partner, but ultimately “decided to focus on its core roadmap” after completing only “some early-stage work.” Also said the grant funding it received from the Shell Foundation “will follow the project to support its ongoing development,” but declined to offer specifics.

The Shell Foundation told TechCrunch in an email that the project was “intended to generate evidence on driver income uplift potential, operational performance and commercial viability to deepen the company’s understanding of the market opportunity.” But when TechCrunch asked for more specifics, the Shell Foundation declined, citing a nondisclosure agreement with Also. Days later, the project disappeared from the Shell Foundation’s website.

During an interview last month at TechCrunch Disrupt, Also co-founder and president Chris Yu said the Kenya pilot project initially made sense given Also’s mission to build small, purpose-built vehicles that are “first and foremost cost-optimized to do the job that needs to be done in a particular market.”

But other projects took precedence, Yu said, especially the development of small autonomous vehicles — which Also is working on as part of a partnership with DoorDash.

“We piloted and ultimately decided, largely because of just urgency and pace around autonomy, frankly, that our attention would be best, in the near term, served fully focused” on that, he said, adding that he thinks there’s a “high chance that autonomy will show up first, and at a broader scale in these types of purpose-built smaller vehicles than at scale in passenger vehicles.”

Also walked away from the Africa project during a somewhat rocky first year of independence.

Supply chain problems forced the company to repeatedly delay deliveries of its first product, a premium e-bike called the TM-B, frustrating customers who had reserved one. What made matters worse was Also’s relative silence. The company said little for much of 2026 about when the bikes would arrive — a communication failure its leadership now acknowledges was a mistake.

“I think we did a pretty poor job communicating to our reservation holders through the summer when they were all waiting, and we got called out for that,” Yu said in the interview. “But I think it’s actually great. It’s really hard to earn the opportunity for people to care, and to tell us what they think, and to help us improve.”

Getting its first product launch back on track is crucial for Also, which has ambitions far beyond e-bikes. The company plans to sell commercial cargo bikes to companies like Amazon, including four-wheeled models, and has the partnership with DoorDash. These products are next in the company’s pipeline, Yu said, and represent bigger revenue opportunities.

But the TM-B comes first. It’s Also’s most visible product to consumers, and its striking design has drawn plenty of curiosity.

Yu said no single problem was responsible for delaying the bikes, which finally started shipping to customers in early October. Instead, Also spent much of the year playing supply chain Whac-A-Mole, a particularly difficult challenge given the TM-B’s complexity. Yu described the bike as “kind of a computer on wheels.”

At one point, Also found itself competing for the same raw materials used to make printed circuit boards for AI data centers. At other times, the company struggled to navigate certification requirements with different government agencies.

Yu said the scope of these problems, and the pace at which new ones popped up — almost weekly — made it difficult to give customers reliable updates about why their bikes were delayed.

“The entire team is like running at a million miles an hour to get these things produced and shipped to customers, and then it’s also really dynamic as well,” he said. “I think what we could have done better is just [say], straight up: ‘We’re chasing down these things, we’ll have an update shortly.’”

That didn’t happen at first, but Also has steadily improved its communication, earning some goodwill from customers on Reddit. The company will need it as it works through the inevitable kinks that come with a first product. Early customers have already reported problems, including delivery damage and noticeable battery drain.

#5303. AI inference startup Fal doubles its valuation to $16B as demand surges

Fal, a San Francisco-based startup that hosts and runs AI video, image, and audio models, has raised $1.3 billion in its latest funding round led by Bessemer Venture Partners, with participation from Nvidia, Sound Ventures, and T. Rowe Price. The deal values Fal at $16 billion, double its $8 billion valuation in April, Bloomberg reported.

The startup announced its Series E and F rounds at the same time, noting that a combined $1.65 billion was raised across both. (Sequoia led the earlier round.)

The latest round (Series F) comes amid soaring demand for inference services, the process of running an AI model that’s already been trained to generate outputs, particularly from customers relying on open source models. Fal surpassed $800 million in annualized revenue earlier this year, Bloomberg’s report noted.

Companies providing inference services, including Baseten, Fireworks AI, and Modal, have also been growing rapidly and raising large funding rounds at higher valuations. But their gross margins remain thin because of the high cost of buying or leasing compute, according to several people familiar with inference companies’ financials.

Fal was co-founded in 2021 by Burkay Gur, a former Coinbase machine learning leader and Oracle engineer, and Gorkem Yurtseven, who was previously a developer at Amazon.

#5300. Ripple's Schwartz Speaks Out About His Influence Over XRP Price

David Schwartz, former chief technology officer of Ripple and one of the original XRP Ledger architects, has responded to claims that he is partially to blame for XRP's poor performance.

In a recent interaction on the X social media platform, David Schwartz was challenged about his possible impact on the price of the Ripple-linked cryptocurrency.

"Don't run from this. You can honestly say you don't have anything to do with it? It's not unfounded anger," the user wrote.

Although David Schwartz does not entirely deny that he can have an impact on the price of XRP, he is clear that it is minimal.

"Can I honestly say that I have nothing to do with the price of XRP? I guess probably not nothing. But very little," David Schwartz responded.

The response from Schwartz comes in the wake of mounting anger within the XRP community about the token's long-running price slump.

Indeed, XRP has seen roughly a 50% decline in value over the past year, per data from CoinMarketCap. During this period, the token has seen several temporary spikes, but the overall trend has been downward.

Of course, XRP is not the only token experiencing such a dramatic drop in value.

Stellar (XLM), another prominent cryptocurrency that seeks to enable payments, has seen a very similar price trend over the same time period.

The interaction came on the back of a long post in which Schwartz lamented the rise in hostile replies he receives on X.

Schwartz, a Ripple veteran, disclosed that some users are actually following him into other discussions and then proceeding to either label him a fraud or criticize him for his work on XRP.

The Ripple veteran noted that he has now made the decision to block such users, as irrelevant crypto-related posts are disrupting his discussions with other users.

Nonetheless, he stressed that the decision affects both critics and fans. Even if someone makes a positive comment about XRP but in an unsuitable place, they might also get blocked.

He also emphasized that he has no issue with honest criticism or accusations that make sense and come with good arguments.

He is mostly annoyed with users who keep hijacking unrelated discussions to vent their frustration.

In fact, Schwartz even offered to unblock users who commit to not doing so in the future.

Schwartz stepped away from his day-to-day duties at Ripple at the end of 2025. He had worked at the firm for over a decade. However, he has not completely left Ripple.

Earlier this month, Schwartz clarified that he's still on Ripple's board of directors and holds the honorary title of CTO Emeritus.

Furthermore, he disclosed that he still meets with his old team twice a month.

#5298. Binance's CZ Calls for Crypto Industry Unity

Former Binance CEO Changpeng Zhao (CZ) is pleading for more unity in the cryptocurrency space, claiming that bickering between different crypto factions doesn't make much sense as digital assets are tightly connected.

"Most crypto assets go up and down together. % might vary a bit, but what's happening to one affects everyone. In-fighting in this space makes zero sense," CZ tweeted.

He capped the post with a simple message pleading for unity: "We need to be: decentralized but united."

CZ was reacting to a social media post that pointed out how crises involving exchanges in the past had affected their respective tokens' prices.

The post pointed to the FTX fiasco in 2022, the WazirX hack in 2024, and the recent security breach at Bitget as examples of how troubles at exchanges can result in significant market losses.

The discussion even pointed to the massive hack at Binance on Oct. 29, which makes CZ's plea for more unity across the crypto space all the more relevant.

The crypto space is currently grappling with one of the biggest security breaches in recent memory.

Binance suffered a staggering $6.34 billion hack on Oct. 29 after hackers broke into the exchange's internal wallet signing infrastructure.

Several digital assets, including Bitcoin, Ethereum, XRP, and Solana, were all impacted by the hack.

Binance has assured users that it will bear the losses from the hack, as opposed to passing them along to customers. According to the exchange's update shared on Nov. 3, around $2.85 billion in stolen funds have been frozen or intercepted, while 98% of affected token assets have been replenished.

In recent days, CZ has been quite vocal about cybersecurity threats.

On Nov. 5, he advised crypto traders to revoke API keys for the third-party trading platform SignalPlus after it was reported that there might have been a security breach.

Meanwhile, CZ also warned his followers against fake websites posing as Trust Wallet, stressing that people shouldn't mistake domains ending in ".cam" for legitimate ".com" ones.

Furthermore, he asked iPhone users to ensure that their OS is up to date following reports of vulnerabilities that could leave crypto holders susceptible to malicious attacks.

#5297. SEC Targets Net Capital, Customer Protection and Recordkeeping Rules for Crypto Brokers

AI-assisted summary, reviewed by NullTX editors.

The SEC's crypto broker-dealer proposal, RIN 3235-AN48, is under White House review with no public text. Here is what the four named rules require today and what review means.

Four rules written decades before Bitcoin existed are now sitting at the White House for a crypto rewrite, and nobody outside the SEC has seen a word of the draft. What is known is the list of rules the agency wants to change, and that list says a lot.

The White House's regulatory review office logged the proposal on November 3. According to the Unified Agenda entry for RIN 3235-AN48, the item is titled "Amendments to Broker-Dealer Financial Responsibility and Recordkeeping and Reporting Rules Regarding Crypto Assets." It sits at the proposed rule stage and carries an economically significant designation. The cited legal authority is Sections 15(c) and 17(a) of the Exchange Act, and the entry lists no legal deadline.

The abstract is short. The SEC's Division of Trading and Markets says it is considering recommending that the Commission amend Rules 15c3-1 and 15c3-3 and other financial responsibility rules, along with Rules 17a-3 and 17a-4, to address how they apply to crypto assets. The CFR citation is listed as not yet determined. The entry's timetable also targeted a proposed rule in July 2026, so the package has run later than the agency planned.

That delay is worth a second look. It hints that the drafting proved harder than expected, which fits the subject, since these rules were built for a world of paper certificates and central clearing agents.

Review by the Office of Information and Regulatory Affairs is not an approval. It is an interagency check on a draft the agency intends to propose, and it comes before the Commission votes to publish anything. The SEC, as an independent agency, now submits significant rules to that office under a 2025 executive order, which explains why a securities rule shows up in a White House queue.

"Economically significant" is a defined term. It generally covers a rule expected to have an annual economic effect of $100 million or more, or one that materially affects a sector of the economy. The label signals expected scale, not content or direction. After review, the process continues with a Commission vote, publication of a proposal, a public comment period and, only then, a final rule.

Nothing in the record says what the rules would change. Anyone claiming the rewrite will loosen or tighten requirements is speculating.

Rule 15c3-1 is the net capital rule. It requires broker-dealers to hold a minimum level of liquid capital, and it applies haircuts to the value of proprietary positions so a firm can absorb losses and still meet its obligations to customers.

The SEC staff's FAQ on crypto asset activities already makes clear that broker-dealers can't ignore crypto. When a firm takes a proprietary position in crypto assets, that exposure must be counted in its net capital computation, and digital assets get no carve-out. The open question, and the likeliest subject of rulemaking, is how a volatile asset with no traditional ready market should be valued and haircut. That design choice carries real consequences for how much capital a crypto-active broker has to hold.

Rule 15c3-3 is the customer protection rule. It requires broker-dealers to promptly obtain and maintain physical possession or control of customers' fully paid and excess margin securities, and it calls for periodic reserve computations to safeguard customer cash. It applies only to securities, so crypto assets that aren't securities fall outside it, even when a broker-dealer holds them.

Existing staff guidance has tackled both prongs. The FAQ says a broker-dealer may establish "control" of a crypto asset security through a control location specified in paragraph (c) of the rule. A December 17, 2025 Division statement took up "physical possession," saying the staff wouldn't object if a firm deems itself to have possession under five conditions. Those conditions cover direct access and transfer capability, written policies assessing the underlying ledger, no custody where the firm knows of material security or operational weaknesses, protection of private keys, and contingency plans for events such as 51% attacks, hard forks and airdrops.

Commissioner Peirce's statement on that release urged the Division to move quickly on recommendations for amending Rule 15c3-3 to cover crypto custody. The OIRA package looks like the follow-up. Because staff statements are non-binding, a formal rule would give firms something sturdier to build on.

Rule 17a-3 lists the books and records a broker-dealer must make, including ledgers, blotters and customer account information. Rule 17a-4 governs how long records must be kept and in what form, with electronic records stored in a non-rewriteable, non-erasable format or under an audit-trail alternative.

Crypto complicates both. A transaction's record lives on a public ledger the firm doesn't control, so a rule would need to settle whether onchain data counts as the firm's own record, how wallet addresses and key-custody events should be documented, and how reconciliation against the ledger should be preserved. The Division will likely address those practical points, given that recordkeeping failures rank among the most common triggers for enforcement actions.

The sequence is predictable even if the content isn't. The first signal would be the release of the draft text or a Commission vote to propose. A comment period follows, in which broker-dealers, custodians, exchanges and investor advocates weigh in, and then comes a possible final rule.

The package matters less for any single provision than for what it signals. The SEC appears to be moving from staff FAQs and non-binding statements toward enforceable rules for the plumbing that crypto-active brokers depend on. Net capital, customer asset protection and recordkeeping determine whether a firm can safely hold customer assets, and they set the cost of doing so.

Until the text appears, the useful questions are narrow ones. Will the SEC differentiate between crypto asset securities and other crypto assets? How will it treat custody through third parties? And will capital charges be calibrated to volatility or set conservatively? The answers will show whether broker-dealers become a practical route to crypto custody or remain a niche.

#5295. Roger Ver Buying Bitcoin Cash Again? Suspicious $163,000 Swap Raises Eyebrows

A mysterious $163,000 crypto transaction has fueled rumors that Roger Ver, the controversial Bitcoin evangelist also known as 'Bitcoin Jesus,' may be purchasing Bitcoin Cash (BCH) once more.

According to on-chain analytics platform Onchain Lens, 73.31 Ethereum (ETH) coins were recently swapped for around 655.74 BCH coins (around $163,000) with the help of the decentralized cross-chain protocol THORChain.

Ver was famously an avid proponent of BCH, hailing it as a better option than the original Bitcoin network.

However, Onchain Lens didn't offer definitive proof that the wallet in question belongs to Ver.

Ver, a crypto pioneer who first entered the crypto space in 2011, quickly rose to become one of the most recognizable early Bitcoin advocates.

He was so passionate about the digital asset that he even earned the moniker 'Bitcoin Jesus' for his aggressive promotion of the cryptocurrency.

But as Bitcoin's controversial scaling debate (which ultimately saw the birth of Bitcoin Cash in August 2017) kicked off, Ver's relations with Bitcoin's mainstream community took a hit.

Ver quickly emerged as one of Bitcoin Cash's most vocal champions.

He passionately argued that BCH's larger block sizes and lower fees help keep Bitcoin true to its roots as a peer-to-peer electronic cash system.

For the past year, Roger Ver has been in the news mostly due to his well-publicized legal dispute with the U.S. government.

Back in April 2024, the crypto entrepreneur was arrested in Spain after U.S. authorities accused him of failing to pay roughly $48M in taxes on his massive Bitcoin holdings and transactions.

Ver, who renounced his U.S. citizenship back in 2014, insisted the prosecution was unjust.

He persistently tried to poke holes in the government's argument.

In June 2025, Ver upped the ante even further.

He took Spain to the European Court of Human Rights to contest the country's decision to extradite him to the U.S.

But the feud took a bombshell twist in October 2025.

Ver and the U.S. Justice Department reached a settlement through a deferred prosecution agreement.

The cryptocurrency figure agreed to pay almost $50 million in unpaid taxes, penalties, and interest.
